The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $n\ge2$ and let $(M,g)$ be a compact, connected, nonempty smooth $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary. Let $\nu_{\mathrm{out}}$ be the outward unit normal and let $\nabla$ be the Levi–Civita connection of $g$. The boundary is **strictly convex** when
$$
g(\nabla_w\nu_{\mathrm{out}},w)>0
$$
for every boundary point and every nonzero boundary-tangent vector $w$. Use the curvature convention
$$
R(X,Y)Z=\nabla_X\nabla_YZ-\nabla_Y\nabla_XZ-\nabla_{[X,Y]}Z.
$$
A Jacobi field along a unit-speed geodesic $\gamma$ is a smooth vector field $J$ satisfying $D_t^2J+R(J,\dot\gamma)\dot\gamma=0$, where $D_tJ=\nabla_{\dot\gamma}J$. The manifold has **no conjugate points** if every positive-length unit-speed geodesic segment $\gamma:[a,b]\to M$ has no nonzero Jacobi field with $J(a)=J(b)=0$. It is **nontrapping** if every maximal unit-speed geodesic starting in $M^\circ$ reaches $\partial M$ in finite forward and backward time. The pair $(M,g)$ is a **simple Riemannian background** if its boundary is strictly convex, it has no conjugate points, and it is nontrapping.

When $n=2$, this is the simple-surface convention used for the scalar geodesic X-ray transform on the required inverse-problems page.
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every smooth manifold with boundary has a smooth collar.
Every smooth function or tensor field on a manifold with boundary extends smoothly across each boundary point to some neighbourhood in its double; the extension is not canonical.
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Every open cover of a smooth manifold with boundary admits a smooth partition of unity subordinate to it.

For a supplied Riemannian metric $g$, a **Levi–Civita connection** is an affine connection on $TM$ that is both metric compatible and torsion free, in the senses of [[def-affine-connection-on-a-smooth-manifold]], [[def-metric-compatible-connection-on-a-riemannian-vector-bundle]] and [[def-torsion-tensor-of-an-affine-connection]]. Thus for all local fields
$$Xg(Y,Z)=g(
abla_XY,Z)+g(Y,
abla_XZ),\qquad 
abla_XY-
abla_YX=[X,Y].$$
Existence and uniqueness are proved below from the supplied metric by the Koszul formula. This definition does not choose an arbitrary connection first and does not assume the general connection-existence theorem. In dimension zero the unique tangent-bundle connection satisfies both identities; in dimension one torsion freeness alone imposes no restriction, so metric compatibility remains essential.
Every supplied smooth Riemannian metric on a smooth manifold, including a manifold with boundary, has exactly one Levi–Civita connection. The construction adds no choice assumption.

Let $X$ be a smooth vector field on $M$ and let $p\in M$. Then there exist
$h>0$, an open neighbourhood $U$ of $p$, and a smooth map

$$ \Phi:(-h,h)\times U\to M $$

such that for every $q\in U$, the curve $t\mapsto \Phi(t,q)$ is the unique
integral curve of $X$ on $(-h,h)$ with initial value $\Phi(0,q)=q$.

On a connected Riemannian manifold define $d_g(p,q)=\inf\{L_g(\gamma):\gamma\text{ is piecewise }C^1\text{ from }p\text{ to }q\}$.

Lengths are those of [[def-riemannian-speed-and-length]]. For each pair $p,q$, [[lem-any-two-points-in-a-connected-smooth-manifold-can-be-joined-by-a-piecewise-c-one-curve]] supplies a curve, so the set of lengths is nonempty, contains a finite real number and is bounded below by zero. Applying the least-upper-bound property [[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]] to the negatives gives a finite nonnegative infimum. On the empty connected manifold this defines the empty distance function; there are no pairs to evaluate. No minimizing curve is part of this definition.

The **Riemannian speed** on a $C^1$ piece is $|\dot\gamma(t)|_g=\sqrt{g_{\gamma(t)}(\dot\gamma(t),\dot\gamma(t))}$. Its **length** is $L_g(\gamma)=\sum_j\int_{t_{j-1}}^{t_j}|\dot\gamma(t)|_g\,dt$.

The curve convention is [[def-piecewise-c-one-curve-on-a-manifold]] and the norm is [[def-pointwise-norm-and-angle-from-a-riemannian-metric]]. Each integrand is continuous on its closed piece with the one-sided endpoint derivative, hence Riemann integrable and nonnegative. Values chosen at the finitely many corners do not change its integral. For a singleton interval the empty sum is zero; a constant curve also has zero length. Partition independence is established by [[lem-riemannian-length-is-independent-of-piecewise-c-one-subdivision]].

The **pointwise norm** is $|v|_g=\sqrt{g(v,v)}$. For nonzero $v,w$ in the same tangent space, the **angle** is the unique $\theta\in[0,\pi]$ with $\cos\theta=g(v,w)/(|v|_g|w|_g)$.

Positive definiteness in [[def-riemannian-metric-and-riemannian-manifold]] makes both denominators positive. [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-for-real-and-complex-inner-product-spaces]] places the quotient in $[-1,1]$, on which the inverse of cosine restricted to $[0,\pi]$ is defined. Angles $0$ and $\pi$ are included. The norm of zero is zero; no angle is assigned when either vector is zero.

For a compact set $K$ contained in one coordinate chart of an $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold, there are $0<c\le C<\infty$ such that $c|v|^2\le g_x(v,v)\le C|v|^2$ for $x\in K$. The dimension-zero assertion is vacuous.
$d_g$ is a finite metric on a connected Riemannian manifold.

Let $(X,d)$ be a metric space ([[def-metric-space]]) and let $\mathcal{T}_d$ be
its metric topology ([[def-metric-topology]]), so that $(X, \mathcal{T}_d)$ is a
topological space ([[def-topological-space]]) and is metrizable
([[def-metrizable-space]]). Then:

1. $(X,d)$ is a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]]) **if and only
   if** $(X, \mathcal{T}_d)$ is a compact topological space
   ([[def-compact-space]]).
2. For every $A \subseteq X$: $A$ is a compact subset of the metric space
   $(X,d)$ if and only if $A$ is a compact subset of the topological space
   $(X, \mathcal{T}_d)$, the two readings of "compact subset" being the metric
   subspace $(A, d_A)$ ([[def-isometry-and-metric-embedding]]) and the topological
   subspace $(A, (\mathcal{T}_d)_A)$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]]).

**Nothing here is a coincidence and nothing is transported.** The open-cover
condition of [[def-metric-compactness]] quantifies over families of subsets open
in $(X,d)$, and by [[def-metric-topology]] those are exactly the members of
$\mathcal{T}_d$; so the two conditions are not merely equivalent, they are the
same condition written twice. No choice principle is used.

Let $(X,d)$ be a compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]). Then $(X,d)$ is totally bounded
([[def-totally-bounded]]) and complete ([[def-complete-metric-space]]).

**Both implications are theorems of ZF.** Completeness is obtained here from the
finite intersection characterisation ([[thm-compact-iff-finite-intersection-property]])
applied to the closures of the tails of a Cauchy sequence, and not from the
extraction of a convergent subsequence, which would route the argument through
sequential compactness. What matters for the ledger is that the route taken below
selects nothing at all; the first remark below says why the other route was not
taken.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $(M,g)$ be a **nonempty**, connected,
boundaryless Riemannian manifold, and let $d=d_g$ be its Riemannian distance.
The following conditions are equivalent.

1. The metric space $(M,d)$ is complete.
2. The Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$ is geodesically complete.
3. For every $p\in M$, the fibre exponential domain is all of the tangent
   space: $\mathcal E_p=T_pM$.
4. There is a point $p_0\in M$ for which $\mathcal E_{p_0}=T_{p_0}M$.
5. Every closed bounded subset of the metric space $(M,d)$ is compact.

Whenever these conditions hold, every $x,y\in M$ are joined by a minimizing
geodesic. More exactly, there is $v\in T_xM$ with
$$
\exp_x(v)=y,\qquad |v|_{g_x}=d(x,y),
$$
and $t\mapsto\exp_x(tv)$ on $[0,1]$ has length $d(x,y)$.

The nonemptiness hypothesis is essential for this formulation: on the empty
manifold conditions 1--3 and 5 are vacuous, whereas condition 4 is false.

Let $a<b$. Suppose $G:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is continuous on $[a,b]$ and differentiable on $(a,b)$. If $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is Riemann integrable and

$$f(x)=G'(x)\qquad(a<x<b),$$

then

$$\int_a^b f=G(b)-G(a).$$

No derivative of $G$ at either endpoint is assumed, and the two endpoint values assigned to the integrable extension $f$ do not enter the conclusion.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be
$C^1$, and let $a\in U$.  If $Df(a)$ is invertible, then there are open sets
$V,W\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $a\in V\subseteq U$ and $f(a)\in W$ such that
$f|_V:V\to W$ is bijective.  Its inverse $g:W\to V$ is $C^1$, and

$$Dg(y)=Df(g(y))^{-1}\qquad(y\in W).$$

Thus $f$ is a local diffeomorphism at $a$.

If $M$ has dimension $n\ge1$, the restrictions of boundary charts to their faces give $\partial M$ the structure of a closed embedded smooth boundaryless $(n-1)$-manifold. For $n=0$, $\partial M=\varnothing$.

For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]]) and every family
$(X_k)_{k < n}$ of compact topological spaces ([[def-compact-space]],
[[def-topological-space]]), the product

$$\prod_{k < n} X_k$$

with the product topology ([[def-product-topology]]) is compact. In particular a
binary product $X \times Y$ of compact spaces is compact, and the empty product,
a one-point space, is compact.

**No choice principle is used beyond [[lem-finite-choice]]**, which is a theorem
of ZF. That is what separates the finite case from the arbitrary one, where the
Axiom of Choice is genuinely spent.

For vectors $u,v$ in a real or complex inner product space,

$$|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\lVert u\rVert\lVert v\rVert.$$

Equality holds if and only if $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent, including the case in which either vector is zero.

derivations.claim: Use [F2] to attach the smooth cylinder $[0,\infty)\times\partial M$ to $M$ along its boundary. By [F3], the metric coefficients extend smoothly across each boundary point to the double. Compactness of $\partial M$ gives a finite such cover; [F4] patches these local extensions by a smooth partition of unity. After shrinking the collar, the patched tensor remains positive definite, since it agrees with $g$ on $M$ and positive definiteness is open. Solve the geodesic ODE for the extended metric from each boundary point in the outward unit-normal direction. At $(x,0)$ the derivative of $(x,s)\mapsto\exp_x(s\nu_{\mathrm{out}}(x))$ sends $(w,a)$ to $w+a\nu_{\mathrm{out}}(x)$, an isomorphism; [F15] therefore gives local inverse charts along the zero section. A finite subcover gives a common domain where this map is a local diffeomorphism. If no uniform collar width made it injective, there would be distinct pairs $(x_j,s_j)$ and $(y_j,t_j)$ with equal images and $0\le s_j,t_j\downarrow0$; compactness gives subsequences converging to $(x,0)$ and $(y,0)$, equality of the images forces $x=y$, and both pairs then lie in one local inverse chart at $(x,0)$, a contradiction. Thus a uniform outward normal collar exists.

In this normal collar, use $s$ for outward normal distance and write the extended metric as $ds^2+\widetilde h_s$, where $\widetilde h_s$ is a smooth family of metrics on $\partial M$. The Gauss-lemma orthogonality follows by differentiating $G(\partial_s,J)$ along a variation field $J$ of normal geodesics: $D_s\partial_s=0$, $[\partial_s,J]=0$, and metric compatibility give $\partial_sG(\partial_s,J)=\tfrac12J(G(\partial_s,\partial_s))=0$, while the initial value is zero. Also $G(\partial_s,\partial_s)=1$. For tangent fields $X,Y$ transported along this collar, metric compatibility and torsion freeness yield $\partial_s\widetilde h_s(X,Y)=G(\nabla_X\partial_s,Y)+G(X,\nabla_Y\partial_s)$; hence $\tfrac12\partial_s\widetilde h_s|_{s=0}$ is the second fundamental form for the outward normal. By [F1], $\partial_s\widetilde h_s$ is positive definite at $s=0$, and compactness makes it positive definite for $0\le s<2\varepsilon$ for some $\varepsilon>0$.

Choose smooth nonincreasing $\xi_1:[0,\infty)\to[0,1]$ with $\xi_1=1$ on $[0,\varepsilon]$ and $\xi_1=0$ on $[2\varepsilon,\infty)$, and set $\xi_2=1-\xi_1$. Since the family $\widetilde h_s/s$ is bounded relative to the positive metric $\widetilde h_0$ on the compact transition interval $[\varepsilon,2\varepsilon]\times\partial M$, choose $C>0$ large enough that $sk-\widetilde h_s$ is positive semidefinite there for $k=C\widetilde h_0$. Define $h_s=\xi_1(s)\widetilde h_s+s\xi_2(s)k$. This is positive definite: on $[0,\varepsilon]$ it equals $\widetilde h_s$, on $[2\varepsilon,\infty)$ it equals $sk$, and on the transition both terms are positive semidefinite with positive-definite sum.

Differentiate the definition to obtain $\partial_sh_s=\xi_1\partial_s\widetilde h_s+\xi_2k+\xi_2'(sk-\widetilde h_s)$. Each term is positive semidefinite on the transition interval, and at least one of the first two is positive definite at every point; outside the transition, $\partial_sh_s=\partial_s\widetilde h_s>0$ near $s=0$ and $\partial_sh_s=k>0$ for $s\ge2\varepsilon$. Thus $\partial_sh_s$ is positive definite for every $s\ge0$. Gluing $ds^2+h_s$ to $g$ gives a smooth Riemannian metric $G$ on the cylinder attachment, because $h_s=\widetilde h_s$ near $s=0$.

Let $p:N\to\mathbb R$ equal $s$ on the cylinder and be smooth and nonpositive on $M$, agreeing with the collar coordinate near $\partial M$; such an extension is obtained by a smooth one-variable cutoff on the compact interior side of the collar. The sublevel set $\{p\le R\}$ is closed by continuity of $p$ and contained in the union of compact $M$ and $[0,\max(R,0)]\times\partial M$, so it is compact by [F16, F17]. The differential of $p$ has bounded metric norm: it has norm $1$ on the cylinder and is bounded on compact $M$. If $C$ is such a bound, then on each $C^1$ piece of a path $\alpha$, [F18] and the chain rule give $|(p\circ\alpha)'|\le C|\dot\alpha|_G$; integrating by [F14] on each piece and summing gives $|p(\alpha(b))-p(\alpha(a))|\le C L_G(\alpha)$. Taking the infimum over paths in [F7] shows that $p$ is $C$-Lipschitz for $d_G$. Hence every $d_G$-Cauchy sequence has bounded $p$ and lies in one compact sublevel set. The metric topology agrees locally with the manifold topology by [F9]: the upper coordinate bound makes nearby coordinate points close in $d_G$, and the lower bound on a smaller chart ball makes any path leaving that ball have a fixed positive length. Thus the sublevel is compact as a metric subspace by [F11], and complete by [F12]. Every Cauchy sequence in $N$ therefore converges in $N$, so $(N,G)$ is complete.

The manifold $N$ is connected, nonempty, and boundaryless, so [F13] extends every geodesic from its initial data to all $t\in\mathbb R$. Let $\gamma$ start at $\partial M$ with unit outward or tangent velocity, and put $r(t)=s(\gamma(t))$ while it is in the exterior. From $G=ds^2+h_s$, the Levi–Civita formula gives $\operatorname{Hess}_G s(\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma)=\tfrac12(\partial_sh_s)(\dot\gamma_T,\dot\gamma_T)\ge0$, where $\dot\gamma_T$ is the component tangent to the level set $\{s=\mathrm{constant}\}$. Thus $r''(t)\ge0$. If $r'(0)>0$, then $r'(t)\ge r'(0)$ and $r(t)>0$ grows without bound. If $r'(0)=0$, then $\dot\gamma(0)$ is a nonzero boundary-tangent vector and strict convexity gives $r''(0)>0$; continuity makes $r'(t)>0$ for some sufficiently small $t>0$, after which the same convexity estimate keeps $r'$ positive and $r(t)\to\infty$. In either case the geodesic never returns to $M$ and eventually leaves every compact subset of $N$.

A **Riemannian metric** on a Hausdorff second-countable smooth manifold $M$ is a smooth symmetric covariant two-tensor $g$ such that $g_p(v,v)>0$ for every point $p$ and every nonzero $v\in T_pM$. A **Riemannian manifold** is the pair $(M,g)$.

This is a [[def-smooth-tensor-field]] giving a [[def-smooth-bundle-metric]] on $TM$. Dimension zero is allowed: its zero bilinear form is positive definite because there are no nonzero vectors. The empty manifold has its unique empty metric. Boundaries are allowed where stated, with smoothness understood up to the boundary.

The **Riemannian volume density** is $\mu_g=\sqrt{\det G_x}\,|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$ in coordinates.

The matrix is that of [[prop-coordinate-criterion-for-a-riemannian-metric]], so its determinant is positive and smooth. The density frames and their absolute-Jacobian law are [[def-density-bundle-and-smooth-density]]. In dimension zero take the empty determinant to be one, giving weight one at every point, independently of orientation. nonempty and let $x, y \in X$. Then

$$|d(x,A) - d(y,A)| \le d(x,y),$$

with $d(\cdot,A)$ the distance to a nonempty set ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
Thus the real-valued function $u \mapsto d(u,A)$ changes by at most $d(u,v)$
between $u$ and $v$: it is **$1$-Lipschitz**.

Let $f:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$.

1. If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, differentiable on $(a,b)$, and $f'$ extends
   continuously to $[a,b]$, then $f$ is Lipschitz.
2. Every Lipschitz $f$ is absolutely continuous.
3. Every absolutely continuous $f$ is continuous and has bounded variation.

Thus, with $C^1$ understood in the endpoint-extension sense of claim 1,
$C^1\subseteq\mathrm{Lipschitz}\subseteq AC\subseteq C\cap BV$ on a compact
interval.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. If $F\in AC[a,b]$, then $F'$ exists almost everywhere on $(a,b)$ and belongs to
$L^1[a,b]$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to \mathbb C$ belong to
$L^1(\mu \times \nu)$. Then:

1. for $\mu$-almost every $x$, the section $f_x$ belongs to $L^1(\nu)$;
2. for $\nu$-almost every $y$, the section $f^y$ belongs to $L^1(\mu)$;
3. after assigning the value $0$ on the exceptional parameter sets, the
   section-integral functions are integrable; and
4. the three integrals agree:
$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$, let
$u,v\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$, and let
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$ be the multi-index of
[[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. We say that $v$ is
the **weak derivative** $D^\alpha u$ if
$$\int_\Omega u\,D^\alpha\varphi\,dx =(-1)^{|\alpha|}\int_\Omega v\varphi\,dx \qquad\text{for every }\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega).$$
Both integrals are finite because the test and all its derivatives are bounded
and compactly supported. The test identity is choice-free. By
[[def-locally-integrable-function-as-a-regular-distribution]] and the signed
transpose convention in [[def-distributional-derivative]], it is equivalent
to $\partial^\alpha T_u=T_v$ as distributions. For $\alpha=0$, this identity
reduces to $T_u=T_v$, hence to $u=v$ almost everywhere by the published
embedding theorem under [[def-countable-choice]].

**Well-definedness.** Changing either representative on a null set leaves each
test integral unchanged. Weak derivatives are therefore statements about
almost-everywhere classes; existence and uniqueness of their locally
integrable value classes are audited separately.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, with
$n\ge1$, and let all functions below be real- or complex-valued classes in
$L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$. Weak differentiation is complex-linear wherever
the derivatives exist: if $v_j=D^\alpha u_j$ weakly for $j=1,2$ and
$a,b\in\mathbb C$, then
$$av_1+bv_2=D^\alpha(au_1+bu_2)\quad\text{weakly}.$$
If $v=D^\alpha u$ weakly on $\Omega$ and $V\subseteq\Omega$ is open, then
$$v|_V=D^\alpha(u|_V)\quad\text{weakly on }V.$$

For the commutation assertion, let $u\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$ and
$\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb N_0^n$. Suppose that the weak derivatives
$$v=D^\alpha u,\qquad w=D^\beta u$$
exist in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$. Then the following three existence
conditions are equivalent: $D^\beta v$ exists in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$;
$D^\alpha w$ exists in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$; and
$D^{\alpha+\beta}u$ exists in $L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$. Whenever they
exist, their value classes are equal almost everywhere on $\Omega$.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, every class is zero, so all these statements hold.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open, $n\ge1$,
$\alpha\in\mathbb N_0^n$, and $u,v,w\in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\Omega)$. If both
$v$ and $w$ are weak $\alpha$-derivatives of $u$, then
$$v=w\quad\text{almost everywhere on }\Omega.$$
Thus a weak derivative, when it exists, is unique as an almost-everywhere
class. No connectedness assumption is needed.

If $\Omega=\varnothing$, the assertion holds because there is only the zero
class and no nonzero tests.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]) and let $T : \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^n$ be linear
with matrix $A$ ([[def-linear-map]],
[[lem-euclidean-linear-maps-have-matrices-and-are-bounded]]).

1. **Invertible case.** If $\det A \ne 0$, then $T[E]$ is Lebesgue measurable for
   every Lebesgue measurable $E$ and
   $$\lambda_n\big(T[E]\big) \;=\; |\det A|\;\lambda_n(E),$$

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space, let $p,q\in[1,\infty]$ be
conjugate exponents, and let $f,g$ be measurable real-valued functions.

1. If $1\le p<\infty$ and $q<\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ and

   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_p\|g\|_q.$$
2. If $p=1$ and $q=\infty$ with $f\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$ and
   $g\in L^\infty(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_1\|g\|_\infty.$$

   $g\in\mathcal L^1(\mu)$, then
   $$\int |fg|\,d\mu\le\|f\|_\infty\|g\|_1.$$

In every case the right-hand side is finite, so $fg$ is integrable.

Then $\eta_\delta(z)=\chi(\sigma(z)/\delta)$ equals one for $t\le\delta/C$, vanishes for $t\ge2\delta/c$, and obeys $|D^\alpha\eta_\delta|\le B_\alpha t^{-|\alpha|}$ on its transition, with constants independent of $\delta$.

For each integer $k\ge1$, take the actual extension $H_k$ produced by [F1]'s fixed cube formula for $P_a^k$. It is $C^k$ everywhere and smooth off $A$, since there it is a locally finite sum of smooth partition functions times polynomials. All these extensions are thereby specified without selecting elements of unspecified nonempty sets. Put $\Delta_k=H_{k+1}-H_k$. It is $C^k$ and all its derivatives through order $k$ vanish on $A$. Taylor's formula at a nearest point of $A$, on a fixed compact neighborhood of $A$, gives for every $|\beta|\le k$ $$|D^\beta\Delta_k(z)|=o(t^{k-|\beta|})\qquad(t=\operatorname{dist}(z,A)\downarrow0),$$ uniformly near $A$. In the parameter-family case these remainders are uniform: the finite-order cube proof bounds $D^\alpha H_k-D^\alpha P_{a_z}^k$ by a constant times the specified Whitney remainder modulus; away from $A$ on a compact set its locally finite formula bounds every derivative by the coefficient bounds. The product rule and step 1.1 show that, for $|\alpha|\le k$, $D^\alpha(\eta_\delta\Delta_k)$ is bounded by a constant $B_k$ times $\max_{|\beta|\le k}t^{|\beta|-|\alpha|}|D^\beta\Delta_k|$, wherever $\eta_\delta$ is nonzero. Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space, let $a$ be a bounded coercive sesquilinear form on $H$ with constants $M,\alpha$ ([[def-bounded-coercive-and-symmetric-sesquilinear-forms]]), and let $F:H\to\mathbb K$ be a bounded conjugate-linear functional with norm $\|F\|=\sup_{\|v\|\le1}|F(v)|$. Then there is a unique $u\in H$ with $$a(u,v)=F(v)\qquad\text{for every }v\in H,$$ and it satisfies $\alpha\|u\|\le\|F\|$, that is $\|u\|\le\|F\|/\alpha$. The real bilinear case is the same statement with $a$ symmetric or not, $F$ a bounded linear functional, and the conjugation read as the identity.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $H$ be a
real or complex Hilbert space ([[def-hilbert-space]]) and let
$T\in\mathcal B(H)$ be a compact self-adjoint operator
([[def-compact-linear-operator]],
[[def-self-adjoint-positive-unitary-and-normal-operator]],
[[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). Let

$$\Sigma:=\{\lambda:\lambda\ \text{is an eigenvalue of}\ T,\ \lambda\ne0\}$$

be its set of nonzero eigenvalues
([[def-eigenvalue-eigenvector-eigenspace-and-spectrum]]), with eigenspaces
$E_\lambda=\ker(T-\lambda I)$ for $\lambda\in\Sigma$. Then:

1. $\Sigma$ is a finite or countably infinite set of **real** numbers, each
   eigenvalue has finite multiplicity in the sense $\dim E_\lambda<+\infty$, and
   for every real $\varepsilon>0$ there are only finitely many
   $\lambda\in\Sigma$ with $|\lambda|\ge\varepsilon$; in particular every point
   of $\mathbb F\setminus\{0\}$ has a neighbourhood containing only finitely
   many elements of $\Sigma$, so the only possible accumulation point of
   $\Sigma$ is $0$;
2. the closed linear span $M$ of $\bigcup_{\lambda\in\Sigma}E_\lambda$ satisfies
   $$M=(\ker T)^\perp=\overline{\operatorname{ran}T}$$
   ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]), and $H=M\oplus M^\perp$
   with $M^\perp\subseteq\ker T$;
3. for every $x\in H$ the finite-subset net of $\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x$
   over the orthogonal projections $P_\lambda$ onto $E_\lambda$ converges in
   norm and
   $$Tx=\sum_{\lambda\in\Sigma}\lambda P_\lambda x ;$$
4. if in addition $H$ is a complex Hilbert space, then the nonzero spectrum
   agrees with the nonzero eigenvalues,
   $$\sigma(T)\cap\{\mu\in\mathbb C:\mu\ne0\}=\Sigma .$$

No Hilbert basis of $\ker T$ is selected anywhere: only the orthonormal bases of
the finite-dimensional eigenspaces $E_\lambda$, $\lambda\ne0$, are used.

derivations.claim: On each of finitely many relatively compact coordinate charts, metric eigenvalues and the volume density have positive lower and finite upper bounds. Thus the intrinsic $H^1$ norm is equivalent to the sum of coordinate $H^1$ norms of a fixed smooth partition of unity. A Cauchy sequence has $L^2$ limits for the localized functions and their first derivatives; testing against a smooth function and passing to the limit identifies the derivative limits as the weak derivatives of the function limit. This proves completeness; $V$, being a closure, is closed. Moreover $1\le q+c\le1+2\|q\|_\infty$, so $b$ and the $H^1$ inner product have equivalent norms. Local mollification of compactly supported functions and a finite partition prove density of $V$ in $H$.

The inclusion $V\hookrightarrow H$ is compact without an arbitrary-index choice argument. Indeed, a localized $v\in V$ extends by zero across a flattened boundary: approximate in $H^1$ by localized interior smooth functions, extend those, and pass to the weak-derivative identities. All extensions have bounded support in a fixed coordinate box. On a cube $C$ of side $\delta$, successively average in its $n$ coordinate variables. The one-variable identity $f(s)-f(t)=\int_t^s f'(r)dr$ and Cauchy–Schwarz give $\|f-\operatorname{avg}_C f\|_{L^2(C)}\le n\delta\|Df\|_{L^2(C)}$ by telescoping those averages; density extends this to $H^1$. Replacement by the mean on each cube of a fixed finite grid is therefore a finite-rank approximation to each coordinate inclusion, with error $O(\delta)$ uniformly on the $H^1$ unit ball. Sum the finitely many coordinate reconstructions to approximate $V\hookrightarrow H$ in operator norm by finite-rank maps. A bounded finite-dimensional set has finite nets; choosing $\delta=2^{-k}$ makes the inclusion's image totally bounded, and completeness of $H$ makes its closure compact. Only countably many finite nets are involved.

In a coordinate chart $Av=f$ is $$-\partial_i(\rho g^{ij}\partial_jv)+\rho qv=\rho f,\qquad \rho=\sqrt{\det g}.$$ The principal matrix is smooth uniformly positive on each compact chart. Localize by a smooth cutoff; its commutator with $A$ has order one. In a boundary chart flatten to $x_n\ge0$ and localize away from the chart sides. The localization can be regarded as a zero-Dirichlet function on a bounded smooth domain agreeing with the half-space near its support and rounded elsewhere. Applying [F3] and the same interior estimate, then summing the finite cover, gives $\|v\|_{H^2}\le C(\|f\|_2+\|v\|_{H^1})$. Testing the equation with $v$ gives $\|v\|_{H^1}\le C(\|f\|_2+\|v\|_2)$ by absorbing the gradient term, so this is the stated $k=0$ estimate.

For $f\in H$, use [F1] to solve $b(Kf,v)=(f,v)_H$. The map $K:H\to V$ is bounded, and step 2.1 makes $K:H\to H$ compact. Symmetry gives $(Kf,h)_H=b(Kf,Kh)=(f,Kh)_H$, positivity gives $(Kf,f)_H=b(Kf,Kf)>0$ for $f\ne0$, and density of $V$ makes $K$ injective. Its range is dense since a vector orthogonal to the range lies in the kernel by self-adjointness. Apply [F2] to obtain positive eigenvalues $\kappa_j\to0$ and a complete $H$-orthonormal family; put $\mu_j=\kappa_j^{-1}$. Repeated finite multiplicities are included. The vectors $e_j/\sqrt{\mu_j}$ are $b$-orthonormal and complete in $V$: if $b(v,e_j)=0$ for every $j$, then $(v,e_j)_H=0$ for every $j$, hence $v=0$. Orthogonal projection and completeness therefore give the asserted $b$-Parseval identity and convergence of the spectral projections in $V$.

Here is the boundary induction for higher orders. Suppose $f\in H^k$ and $v\in H^{k+1}$ is already known. In a flattened boundary chart apply a tangential derivative $D_{x'}^\alpha$, $|\alpha|=k$, to the localized equation. Its commutator with the second-order operator contains derivatives of $v$ of order at most $k+1$ with bounded smooth coefficients. The localized $D_{x'}^\alpha v$ has zero trace and lies in $H^1$; this follows first for tangential difference quotients, which preserve zero trace, and then by their $H^1$ limit. The $k=0$ local estimate of step 2.2 gives its $H^2$ bound in terms of $\|f\|_{H^k}+\|v\|_{H^{k+1}}$. If a derivative has total order $k+2$ and at least three normal factors, differentiate the equation $k$ times, isolating the term $\rho g^{nn}D_n^2v$. Divide by the positive coefficient $\rho g^{nn}$. Each other highest-order derivative has fewer normal factors because its two principal derivatives include a tangential derivative; all commutators have order at most $k+1$. Induction on the number of normal factors therefore bounds every derivative of order $k+2$. Interior patches allow derivatives in all directions. Difference quotients justify each differentiation before regularity is established; the bounds are uniform in their increments, and testing their weak limits identifies the claimed derivatives. Nested cutoffs and the finite cover give $\|v\|_{H^{k+2}}\le C_k(\|f\|_{H^k}+\|v\|_{H^{k+1}})$, and the previous induction level absorbs the last term into $C_k(\|f\|_{H^k}+\|v\|_2)$. This proves all asserted elliptic estimates.

For completeness the needed high-order embedding also has a finite-chart proof with this axiom base. In a half-chart extend across $x_n=0$ by $\sum_{j=1}^{k+1}a_jv(x',-jx_n)$ for $x_n<0$, where the finite Vandermonde system $\sum_j a_j(-j)^\ell=1$ for $0\le\ell\le k$ matches the derivatives at the interface. After a cutoff this is a bounded $H^k$ extension; the assertion follows first on smooth functions and then by the weak derivative identities and approximation. On a bounded support box, iterated one-dimensional integration gives $\|D^\alpha w\|_\infty\le C\|D_1\cdots D_nD^\alpha w\|_2$ for smooth compactly supported $w$. Apply this also to first derivatives of $D^\alpha w$ and to differences of mollifications. For $k\ge n+a+1$ these mollifications and all derivatives through order $a$ are uniformly Cauchy and their limits are continuous, with the asserted norm bound; passing to the coordinate segment integral identifies them as classical derivatives. Sum the finite chart extensions. This proves the embedding and completes the lemma.

derivations.claim: Set $c=1+\|q\|_\infty$, $a(u,v)=b(u,v)-c(u,v)_{L^2}$, and let $P_J$ be projection on $e_1,\ldots,e_J$. Solve the scalar equations $d_j''+(\mu_j-c)d_j=(F,e_j)$ with the projected initial data, and put $u_J=\sum_{j\le J}d_je_j$. The scalar solutions exist for $L^1$ forcing by integration against the sine/hyperbolic-sine fundamental solution (at zero frequency use $t$); they have continuous first derivatives and absolutely continuous first derivatives on compact intervals. For $E_J=(\|u_J'\|_2^2+b(u_J,u_J))/2$, multiply each equation by $\bar d_j'$ and take real parts to obtain $$E_J'=\operatorname{Re}(P_JF+cu_J,u_J')\le C E_J+\sqrt{2E_J}\|F\|_2.$$ Apply this to $\sqrt{E_J+\eta}$ and let $\eta\downarrow0$ after integrating: multiplication by $e^{-Ct}$ gives $\sqrt{E_J(t)}\le C_T(\sqrt{E_J(0)}+\int_0^T\|F\|_2dt)$. This is exactly the asserted estimate, uniformly in $J$.

For $J>K$, the same estimate for $u_J-u_K$ has data $(P_J-P_K)u_0,(P_J-P_K)u_1$ and forcing $(P_J-P_K)F$. These data tend to zero in $V\times H$ by [F1]. The forcing tends to zero in $L^1_tH$ because the projections converge pointwise in $H$ and are contractive, so dominated convergence applies. Hence $u_J$ is Cauchy in $C([0,T];V)$ and $u_J'$ in $C([0,T];H)$. Their limits $u,w$ satisfy $u(t)-u(s)=\int_s^t w(r)dr$, so $u\in C^1([0,T];H)$ with derivative $w$ and the exact strong initial traces. Pass to the limit in the integrated finite-dimensional equation first for a finite spectral test and then for every $\phi\in V$, using boundedness of $a$ and the form-density in [F1]. This gives precisely the displayed weak equation and energy bound. No weak-in-time limiting trace is substituted for a strong trace.

If two energy solutions have the same data and forcing, test their difference against $e_j$. The scalar coefficient is a distributional solution of $d_j''+(\mu_j-c)d_j=0$ with zero strong data. Its integral equation, or the scalar fundamental solution, gives $d_j=0$. Completeness in [F1] makes the difference zero for every time. The estimate of step 1.1 passes to the strong limit, including its zero-data version. Replacing $t$ by $T-t$ proves terminal well-posedness with the same bound.

We also establish the classical regularity needed by the last assertion and the DN interfaces. Let $h$ be smooth and zero near the temporal endpoints, take the smooth lift $H$ from [F2], and solve for $w=u-H$ with zero Dirichlet and initial data and forcing $G=-L_qH$. This $G$ is smooth and zero near $t=0$. For every integer $\ell\ge0$, solve the same zero-data energy problem with forcing $\partial_t^\ell G$. Integration in time and uniqueness in step 3.1 identify these solutions successively with $\partial_t^\ell w$: for example integrating the solution with forcing $G_t$ gives a solution with forcing $G-G(0)=G$ and zero data. Thus all time derivatives of $w$ are continuous in $V$. At every time, $Aw=G-w_{tt}$; the right side is continuous in $L^2$, so [F1]'s elliptic estimate gives continuity of $w$ in $H^2$, by applying the estimate to time differences. Thus all mixed derivatives have arbitrarily high spatial Sobolev regularity, and [F1]'s embedding gives a smooth representative on the closed cylinder, in particular $C^2$. Adding $H$ proves the stated smooth boundary reduction and actual classical forward solvability; time reversal gives the terminal version.

A weak coordinate derivative $D_iw$ is defined by $\int w\,\partial_i\psi=-\int D_iw\,\psi$ for every smooth compactly supported coordinate test $\psi$. Let $H^1(M)$ be the space of $L^2$ functions whose weak coordinate first derivatives are locally $L^2$ in smooth charts and whose weak differential has finite metric $L^2$ norm; write $\nabla_gu$ for the metric dual of that weak differential. Give it norm
$$\|w\|_{H^1(M)}^2=\int_M(|w|^2+|\nabla_gw|_g^2)\,dV_g,$$
and let $H_0^1(M)$ be the closure of $C_c^\infty(M^\circ)$ in this norm. For $u_0\in H_0^1(M)$, $u_1\in L^2(M)$, and $F\in L^1((0,T);L^2(M))$, there is a unique energy solution of the homogeneous Dirichlet problem
$$u_{tt}-\Delta_gu+q(x)u=F,\qquad u|_{(0,T)\times\partial M}=0,\qquad (u(0),u_t(0))=(u_0,u_1),$$

$$u\in C([0,T];H_0^1(M))\cap C^1([0,T];L^2(M)),$$

derivations.claim: Cover the parameter interval by finitely many small overlapping intervals on which the immersed base curve is embedded. The central covector satisfies $p=0$ and $p_{\xi_s}\ne0$, since the Hamilton velocity in these coordinates is a nonzero multiple of $\partial_s$. The formal implicit equation $p(s,y,\partial_s\phi,\partial_y\phi)=0$ can thus be solved recursively for the jets of $\partial_s\phi$. This is an evolution eikonal equation in $s$, with a smooth real reduced Hamiltonian in the real variables. Its zeroth and first jet equations are exactly the given Hamilton curve (after its parameter change). Initialize the transverse Hessian by $H(0)=iI$ in the chosen transverse coordinates.

The quadratic jet equation is the matrix Riccati equation $$H'+D+BH+HB^T+HCH=0,$$ where $C,D$ are real symmetric and $B$ real, the corresponding blocks of the reduced Hamiltonian Hessian. Solve instead $Y'=B^TY+CZ$, $Z'=-DY-BZ$, $Y(0)=I$, $Z(0)=iI$. Direct differentiation gives $Y^TZ-Z^TY=0$ and $Y^*Z-Z^*Y=2iI$. If $Yv=0$ the second identity gives $0=2i|v|^2$, so $Y$ is invertible on the whole interval. Consequently $H=ZY^{-1}$ is symmetric, solves the Riccati equation, and $$\operatorname{Im}H=(Y^{-1})^*Y^{-1}>0.$$ Compactness gives uniform positive lower and finite upper bounds. At an overlap transform all jets by the coordinate chain rule, carry these initial data to the next chart, and use ODE uniqueness. Positivity is unchanged by real coordinate change and persists on the finite cover.

For transverse degree $k\ge3$, differentiating the reduced eikonal equation $k$ times gives a finite linear ODE for the degree-$k$ phase jet: its highest jet enters linearly, with coefficients determined by the Hessian and the first derivatives of the reduced Hamiltonian; the inhomogeneous terms involve only lower jets and derivatives of the symbol. This follows by the product rule: terms containing a highest derivative of $\phi$ can have only one such factor, and the degree-$k+1$ derivative cancels against differentiation along the central Hamilton curve. Thus solve successively for every degree using [F2], matching all jets on overlaps. Apply [F1], or its explicit shrinking-cutoff series, to realize them. This yields a smooth phase with eikonal defect flat on each branch and $\operatorname{Im}\phi\ge c|y|^2$ after shrinking the transverse tube.

Define $T_\phi$ to be the coefficient of $h^{-1}$ in the exact conjugation identity $$P(e^{i\phi/h}a)=e^{i\phi/h}(h^{-2}p(x,d\phi)a+h^{-1}T_\phi a+Pa).$$ It is a first-order operator with derivative part $p_\xi(x,d\phi)\cdot D$, so its coefficient of $\partial_s$ on the ray is nonzero. The central $a_0$ equation is a scalar homogeneous ODE with nonzero initial value, hence has nonvanishing exponential solution. For each successive transverse degree and amplitude index the differentiated equations are linear ODEs with already known right sides, by the same cancellation of derivatives along the curve as in step 3.1. Realize these jets by [F1]. The separate asymptotic series $a(x;h)\sim\sum_{j\ge0}h^ja_j(x)$ is realized by $\sum_jh^ja_j(x)\eta(h/\delta_j)$, with $\eta=1$ near zero and $\delta_j\downarrow0$ chosen so its $C^k$ tails are summable for every fixed $k$ and have the required $h$ asymptotic bounds. derivations.claim: Choose a smooth boundary defining function $\rho$ positive inside. At a tangent unit vector $\omega$ at $x_0$, strict convexity says $(\rho\circ\gamma_\omega)''(0)<0$. Taylor's formula factors the boundary equation as $\rho(\gamma_\omega(s))=s(a+sB(\omega,s))$, with $B<0$ uniformly near tangency. The implicit function theorem gives the first positive exit $\tau(\omega)$ there, with $\tau/a$ extending continuously and positively to tangent directions. Every other exit is transverse: a first exit with zero normal derivative would have $\rho=0$, $\rho'=0$, $\rho''<0$, forcing $\rho<0$ immediately before the exit. Thus all inward exits vary smoothly, and $\tau\to0$ at the equator.

These exit times are uniformly bounded. Otherwise take inward unit directions $\omega_j$ and increasing lengths tending to infinity with no exit before those lengths. Compactness gives a limiting direction. Step 1.1 excludes a tangent limit. Smooth dependence then gives an inward geodesic remaining in $M$ for every positive time, contrary to nontrapping. Define $$B_{x_0}=\{s\omega:\omega\text{ inward unit},\ 0\le s\le\tau(\omega)\},$$ including $0$ and tangent endpoints only as $0$. It is compact. Identify the inward normal with the last Euclidean coordinate and compare this radial set with the closed ball of radius one centred at the inward normal, whose radial length is $2\omega_n$ on the inward hemisphere. The radial map multiplies by $\tau(\omega)/(2\omega_n)$. Step 1.1 makes this ratio extend positively and continuously to the equator, so the radial map and its inverse are continuous also at zero. Hence $B_{x_0}$ is homeomorphic to a closed $n$-ball.

In the complete exterior of [F2], the exponential map $E(v)=\exp_{x_0}(v)$ is smooth on a neighborhood of $B_{x_0}$. Its differential is nonsingular for $v\ne0$ in that set: a kernel vector produces a Jacobi field vanishing at the two endpoints, excluded by [F1]; its radial component cannot be in the kernel since the geodesic has unit speed. At $0$ the differential is the identity. On the radial boundary $s=\tau(\omega)>0$, transversality from step 1.1 identifies $B_{x_0}$ locally with the inverse image of $M$ under this inverse chart, so the restricted map is a local homeomorphism of manifolds with boundary. The same is true at $0$: in a small normal neighborhood the inverse image of $M$ is precisely the short inward radial segments; tangent and outward rays immediately leave by strict convexity, and inward directions with very small exit time have already left. The exterior no-return property excludes extra portions of a ray in this local description. Thus $E:B_{x_0}\to M$ is a local homeomorphism everywhere.

Apply [F3] to this compact radial ball. It is a finite covering of $M$, and its simply connected total space makes it regular. If a fibre had two points, transitivity would supply a nonidentity deck transformation of $B_{x_0}$. Conjugate it by the ball homeomorphism of step 2.1. By [F4] it has a fixed point, and by uniqueness of lifts in [F3] a deck transformation with a fixed point is the identity, a contradiction. Every fibre therefore has one point. A minimizing exterior geodesic from $x_0$ to $y\in M^\circ$ exists by [F5]. It cannot leave $M$ and return, by [F2]; it must start inward, since an outward or tangent launch never enters $M$. Metric compatibility and the Jacobi equation give $(g(D_sJ,\dot\gamma))'=0$, and hence $(g(J,\dot\gamma))'=0$ with zero initial value. The Gauss orthogonality proved in [F1] gives $g=dr^2+g_{\alpha\beta}d\theta^\alpha d\theta^\beta$ and $\Delta_gr=m^{-1}\partial_rm$.

Put $\phi=t-r$, $z=t-r-(t_0-\delta)$, and $D=\partial_t+\partial_r$. Then $\phi_t^2-|\nabla\phi|^2=0$ and, for $L_q=\partial_t^2-\Delta_g+q$, direct differentiation gives $$L_q(e^{i\lambda\phi}a)=e^{i\lambda\phi}(i\lambda\mathcal T a+L_qa),\qquad \mathcal T=2D+\partial_r\log m.$$ The variable $z$ and the angle $\theta$ are constant along $D$, and $D(m^{1/2}a)=m^{1/2}\mathcal T a/2$. Consequently $$a_0=m^{-1/2}\chi_\lambda(\theta,z),\qquad a_{1,q}=\frac{i}{2}m^{-1/2}\int_{r_*}^{r}m(\sigma,\theta)^{1/2}(L_qa_0)(\sigma,\theta,z)\,d\sigma$$ solve $\mathcal T a_0=0$, $\mathcal T a_{1,q}=iL_qa_0$, where all functions in the integral are expressed in $(r,\theta,z)$ and $r_*$ is a fixed exterior radial start. Extend the smooth metric coefficients and the interior potentials over this slightly longer tube. Integration in $r$ preserves support in $(\theta,z)$. The same recursion $\mathcal T a_{j,q}=iL_qa_{j-1,q}$ supplies every higher requested finite order; two amplitude terms already suffice for the stated bound.

Choose the angular and $z$ supports sufficiently small. Transversality of the entry and exit makes the tube's part in $M$ lie between smooth nearby entry and exit radii; all these packets are zero on $M$ near $t=0,T$. Put a radial cutoff equal to one near the entire tube intersection with $M$ and supported with its radial derivatives outside $M$. Then $$v_{+,q}=e^{i\lambda\phi}(a_0+\lambda^{-1}a_{1,q}),\qquad L_qv_{+,q}=\lambda^{-1}e^{i\lambda\phi}L_qa_{1,q}\quad\text{on }Q.$$ On the fixed compact nonsingular tube, coefficient derivatives, integration lengths, and coordinate Jacobians are bounded independently of $\lambda$. The formula in step 2.1 and the chain rule therefore give $\|a_{1,q}\|_{C^k}\le C_k\|\chi_\lambda\|_{W^{k+2,\infty}}$ and $$\|L_qv_{+,q}\|_{L^1_tL^2_x}\le C\lambda^{-1}\|\chi_\lambda\|_{W^{4,\infty}}.$$ For the opposite phase use $v_{-,q}=\overline{v_{+,q}}$ (real $q$), obtaining the identical estimate. In particular the cutoff creates no residual inside the measurement domain.

Apply [F2] to $-L_{q_1}v_{+,q_1}$ with zero initial and boundary data, and to $-L_{q_2}v_{-,q_2}$ with zero terminal and boundary data. The smooth right sides vanish near the relevant time endpoints, so the regularity part of [F2] makes the corrections smooth. The resulting $u_1=v_{+,q_1}+R_1$ and $u_2=v_{-,q_2}+R_2$ are actual forward and terminal classical solutions, with smooth boundary traces compactly supported in time. The energy estimate gives $$\|R_j\|_{L^\infty_tH^1_x}+\|\partial_tR_j\|_{L^\infty_tL^2_x}\le C\lambda^{-1}\|\chi_\lambda\|_{W^{4,\infty}}.$$ Thus the remainder here is the correction to the complete two-term approximate solution, including its $\lambda^{-1}$ transport amplitude.

In local coordinates about $(\theta_0,0)$ let $\zeta\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R)$ satisfy $\int\zeta^2dy=1$, choosing a cutoff Gaussian and dividing by its $L^2$ norm. Set $$\varepsilon=\lambda^{-1/(n+8)},\qquad \chi_\lambda(\theta,z)=\varepsilon^{-n/2}\zeta((\theta-\theta_0,z)/\varepsilon).$$ For bounded small $\lambda$ enlarge the constants and keep the support inside the tube; all asymptotic assertions concern sufficiently large $\lambda$. Then $\|\chi_\lambda\|_2=1$ and $\|\chi_\lambda\|_{W^{k,\infty}}\le C_k\varepsilon^{-n/2-k}$. For $k=4$ the exponent is exactly $\lambda^{1/2}$, so step 4.1 proves $\|R_j\|_{L^2(Q)}=O(\lambda^{-1/2})$. Also $\|a_0\|_{L^2(Q)}\le C$ since its squared metric density cancels $m$, and $$\|\lambda^{-1}a_{1,q}\|_2\le C\lambda^{-1}\varepsilon^{-n/2-2}=o(1).$$ This verifies every normalization and derivative loss used in the correction estimate.

For a smooth test $A$, the leading product is $a_0^2=m^{-1}\chi_\lambda^2$. Since $dt=dz$ at fixed $r$, $$\int_Q A a_0^2\,dV_gdt=\int \chi_\lambda(\theta,z)^2\left[\int_{r_-(\theta)}^{r_+(\theta)} A(r+t_0-\delta+z,x(r,\theta))\,dr\right]d\theta dz.$$ The nearby entry and exit radii are smooth by transversality. The bracket converges uniformly as $(\theta,z)\to(\theta_0,0)$ to $\int_0^L A(t_0+s,\gamma(s))ds$. The change of variables $(\theta-\theta_0,z)=\varepsilon y$ and $\int\zeta^2=1$ prove the required ray limit with coefficient exactly one. The terms containing a $\lambda^{-1}a_{1,q}$ vanish by the $L^2$ bounds in step 5.1 and Cauchy–Schwarz; the terms containing $R_j$ vanish by the same inequality and step 4.1. These arguments also apply to any smooth function on the closed cylinder, not only a compactly supported interior test, because all approximate packets are supported away from the temporal endpoints and the global correction errors have vanishing $L^2$ norm. Thus the exact forward/terminal product has the asserted normalized limit.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a compact, connected, nonempty smooth Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary, let $T>0$, and let $q_1,q_2\in C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ be independent of time. Write $Q=(0,T)\times M$, $\Sigma=(0,T)\times\partial M$, and $P=\partial_t^2-\Delta_g$. For $h,k\in C_c^\infty(\Sigma)$, let $u$ be the zero-initial-data solution for $P+q_1$ with boundary value $h$, and let $v$ be the zero-terminal-data solution for $P+q_2$ with boundary value $k$, in the classical solution classes used to define the forward map $\Lambda_{q_1}^+$ and terminal map $\Lambda_{q_2}^-$; thus $u,v\in C^2([0,T]\times M)$. Then
$$\int_0^T\!\int_M(q_1-q_2)u(t,x)v(t,x)\,dV_g(x)\,dt=\int_0^T\!\int_{\partial M}\big(k\,\Lambda_{q_1}^+h-h\,\Lambda_{q_2}^-k\big)\,dS_g\,dt.$$
The boundary factors are paired bilinearly, without complex conjugation, and each normal derivative is the outward classical normal trace.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a compact, connected, nonempty simple Riemannian background of dimension $n\ge2$, let $T>0$, and let $q_1,q_2\in C_c^\infty(M^\circ;\mathbb R)$ be static potentials. Let $\gamma:[0,L]\to M$ be a maximal unit-speed geodesic with $0<L<T$, and choose a time shift $t_0$ with $0<t_0<T-L$. In a nonsingular geodesic-polar tube about $\gamma$, there are conjugate eikonal phases and transport amplitudes, with a transverse cutoff of width $\varepsilon_\lambda=\lambda^{-1/(n+8)}$, that produce approximate forward and terminal solutions for the two wave operators. After solving the transport hierarchy through the required finite order and correcting the residual by the zero-data energy solver, the exact solutions have remainders $R_{j,\lambda}$ satisfying
$$\|R_{j,\lambda}\|_{L^\infty(0,T;H^1(M))}\le C\lambda^{-1}\|\chi_\lambda\|_{W^{4,\infty}},\qquad \|R_{j,\lambda}\|_{L^2((0,T)\times M)}=O(\lambda^{-1/2}),$$
where $\chi_\lambda$ is the stated transverse cutoff and $C$ is independent of $\lambda$. The normalized product of the forward and terminal exact solutions converges against every compactly supported smooth spacetime test function to integration along the null ray $(t_0+s,\gamma(s))$, $0\le s\le L$, with the Gaussian normalization fixed so that the limiting transverse integral is one.

Assume Countable Choice. Let $(M,g)$ be a compact, connected, nonempty smooth Riemannian manifold with smooth boundary, let $T>0$, and write $Q=(0,T)\times M$ and $\Sigma=(0,T)\times\partial M$. Let $q\in C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$ be independent of time, and let $L_q=\partial_t^2-\Delta_g+q$. Write $\mathcal H=C_c^\infty(\Sigma)$ for smooth Dirichlet data compactly supported away from the temporal endpoints. Assume that for every $h\in\mathcal H$ the zero-initial-data Dirichlet problem $L_qu=0$, $u|_\Sigma=h$, $(u(0),u_t(0))=(0,0)$ has a unique solution $u_{q,h}\in C^2([0,T]\times M)$. Define the full time-dependent Dirichlet-to-Neumann map by
$$\Lambda_q^+ :\mathcal H\to L^2(\Sigma,dS_gdt),\qquad \Lambda_q^+h=\partial_{\nu_{out}}u_{q,h}|_\Sigma,$$
where $\nu_{out}$ is the outward unit normal. Also assume that for every $k\in\mathcal H$ the terminal-data Dirichlet problem $L_qv=0$, $v|_\Sigma=k$, $(v(T),v_t(T))=(0,0)$ has a unique solution $v_{q,k}\in C^2([0,T]\times M)$, and define
$$\Lambda_q^- :\mathcal H\to L^2(\Sigma,dS_gdt),\qquad \Lambda_q^-k=\partial_{\nu_{out}}v_{q,k}|_\Sigma.$$
The Green boundary pairing is the bilinear pairing $\int_\Sigma h\,\partial_{\nu_{out}}v\,dS_gdt$; the classical normal trace is in $L^2(\Sigma)$ for each stated $C^2$ solution class. Equality of two forward maps means equality on every $h\in\mathcal H$ over the whole time interval $(0,T)$, with the analogous convention for terminal maps.

derivations.claim: First use [F1] with both potentials equal to a single real $q$. Its left side is zero, so for every $h,k$ in the boundary input space $$\int_\Sigma k\Lambda_q^+h\,dS_gdt=\int_\Sigma h\Lambda_q^-k\,dS_gdt.$$ This is a bilinear transposition identity and uses exactly the classical forward and terminal solutions, whose endpoint terms vanish. Therefore the right side of [F1] for $q_1,q_2$ equals $\int_\Sigma k(\Lambda_{q_1}^+-\Lambda_{q_2}^+)h\,dS_gdt$, which is zero under the assumed equality of forward maps. Hence $\int_Q(q_1-q_2)uv\,dV_gdt=0$ for every admitted forward $q_1$ wave and terminal $q_2$ wave.

Choose $t_0\in(0,T-L)$ and insert the exact waves of [F2] into step 1.1. Their boundary traces belong to the full input space for each $\lambda$, so the zero identity applies without a limit or density assumption on boundary data. The product convergence of [F2], with $A(t,x)=q_1(x)-q_2(x)$, gives $$0=\lim_{\lambda\to\infty}\int_Q(q_1-q_2)u_{1,\lambda}u_{2,\lambda}\,dV_gdt=\int_0^L(q_1-q_2)(\gamma(s))\,ds.$$ The test is legitimate either by [F2]'s closed-cylinder conclusion or by a temporal cutoff equal to one on all approximate packets; its omitted exact-product terms contain vanishing correction factors. Since the ray was arbitrary subject to $L<T$, every claimed ray integral is determined.
